name: Cryptographic Protocols
description: Design and analysis of cryptographic protocols such as TLS, key exchange, messaging, and PKI.

ndss.narrative:
Cryptographic protocol research at NDSS has maintained a consistent emphasis on exposing weaknesses in widely-deployed standards and then proposing principled fixes. TLS-N (NDSS 2018) extended TLS with non-repudiation; Component-Based Formal Analysis of 5G-AKA (NDSS 2019) was the first rigorous decomposition of the new cellular authentication protocol's channel assumptions, revealing subtle session-confusion issues.

The 2020–2022 period addressed emerging trust challenges: post-quantum readiness entered TLS 1.3 performance studies; Automata-Based Automated Detection of State Machine Bugs (NDSS 2023) systematized the search for implementation flaws in stateful security protocols; and Bluetooth pairing received formal scrutiny (Extrapolating Formal Analysis to Uncover Attacks in Bluetooth Passkey Entry Pairing, NDSS 2023). The recurring theme is that deployed protocols, however carefully specified, harbour implementation-level state-machine divergences.

The most recent papers show two growing concerns: asynchronous Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus (Speeding Dumbo, NDSS 2022) for blockchain-adjacent applications, and post-quantum migration. WireGuard received unified symbolic analysis (A Unified Symbolic Analysis of WireGuard, NDSS 2024), and Recurrent Private Set Intersection for Unbalanced Databases (NDSS 2025) paired efficiency with quantum-resistant primitives. Collectively this body of work charts a course from classical TLS hardening to quantum-safe, formally verified next-generation protocols.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this collection, all from USENIX Security 2018, show a field already split between two recurring concerns: building new cryptographic systems and breaking or formally scrutinizing existing protocols. On the construction side, "Arbitrum: Scalable, private smart contracts" (USENIX 2018) pushed cryptographic machinery toward scalable, privacy-preserving computation, while on the attack side "The Dangers of Key Reuse: Practical Attacks on IPsec IKE" (USENIX 2018) demonstrated that real-world key-establishment standards remained exploitable when keys were shared across modes. Alongside these, "Modelling and Analysis of a Hierarchy of Distance Bounding Attacks" (USENIX 2018) signaled an early commitment to formal, calculus-based reasoning about protocol security — a thread that would only grow stronger.

The next few years marked a clear breakthrough toward automated formal analysis of protocol families rather than one-off proofs. "A Spectral Analysis of Noise" (USENIX 2020) gave a comprehensive automated treatment of the entire Noise family of Diffie-Hellman handshakes, and "SmartVerif" (USENIX 2020) pushed automation further with dynamic verification strategies, while "Analysis of DTLS Implementations Using Protocol State Fuzzing" (USENIX 2020) brought systematic state-machine testing to deployed code. In parallel, the community kept finding that widely trusted deployments leak: "Why Eve and Mallory Still Love Android" (USENIX 2021) showed TLS validation was still broken in mobile apps, "Why TLS is better without STARTTLS" (USENIX 2021) and "ALPACA" (USENIX 2021) exposed cross-protocol and application-layer confusion attacks against TLS, and "Card Brand Mixup Attack" (USENIX 2021) bypassed PINs in EMV payment cards. Secure messaging matured into its own subfield, with "The Complexities of Healing in Secure Group Messaging" (USENIX 2021) formalizing post-compromise security across groups and "Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G" (USENIX 2021) hardening cellular authentication.

By 2022–2023 the work fused rigorous cryptanalysis with the messengers and databases people actually use. "Breaking Bridgefy, again" (USENIX 2022) showed that adopting libsignal does not automatically yield security, and "Three Lessons From Threema" (USENIX 2023) delivered a full cryptographic teardown of a ten-million-user messenger. The same period broadened the scope to encrypted databases and large-scale TLS hygiene, with "Security Analysis of MongoDB Queryable Encryption" (USENIX 2023) and "We Really Need to Talk About Session Tickets" (USENIX 2023) measuring real cryptographic dangers at scale, while "Linear Private Set Union" (USENIX 2023) advanced efficient privacy-preserving set operations.

Most recently the field has turned to the post-quantum transition and cross-chain settings while keeping its formal-methods backbone. "Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol" (USENIX 2024) verified Signal's new post-quantum handshake before wide deployment — a direct descendant of the automated-analysis line begun around 2020 — and "Parallelizing Universal Atomic Swaps for Multi-Chain Cryptocurrency Exchanges" (USENIX 2025) extends secure-protocol design into trustless cross-blockchain exchange. Across these venues the trajectory is consistent: from isolated attacks and constructions, to automated analysis of whole protocol families, to rigorous study of mass-deployed messengers and databases, and now to post-quantum and multi-chain protocols verified before they ship.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, from 2018, already reveal that "cryptographic protocols" at the top venues had split into two big currents. One current is the explosion of blockchain and distributed-ledger work: OmniLedger (S&P 2018) and RapidChain (CCS 2018) both attacked the scalability problem by sharding a permissionless ledger so it could approach Visa-like throughput, while Arbitrum (USENIX 2018) tackled smart contracts that are both scalable and private. The other current is classic protocol design and analysis: practical threshold ECDSA with trustless setup (CCS 2018) and two-party threshold ECDSA from standard assumptions (S&P 2018) made distributed signing deployable, and secure-computation work like Compressing Vector OLE (CCS 2018) and HyCC (CCS 2018) pushed MPC toward practicality. At the same time, attack-and-analysis papers grounded the field in reality: The Dangers of Key Reuse exposed practical attacks on IPsec IKE (USENIX 2018), and formal modeling appeared via the distance-bounding analysis (USENIX 2018).

By 2019-2020 the field matured along both lines. On consensus and BFT, Flexible BFT (CCS 2019) and Sync HotStuff (S&P 2020) simplified and strengthened Byzantine fault tolerance, setting up the throughput-focused designs that followed. Formal verification became a marquee result, with the component-based analysis of 5G-AKA (NDSS 2019) finding flaws in a standard headed for billions of devices, echoed on the implementation side by protocol state fuzzing of DTLS (USENIX 2020). Real-world breakage stayed prominent through Dragonblood against WPA3's Dragonfly handshake (S&P 2020) and BIAS impersonation attacks on Bluetooth (S&P 2020). Meanwhile threshold cryptography and distributed key generation moved from theory to systems: Asynchronous DKG (CCS 2020) and Towards Scalable Threshold Cryptosystems (S&P 2020) made the trusted-dealer assumption avoidable at scale, and DECO (CCS 2020) cleverly turned TLS sessions into provable oracles of web data.

From 2021 onward the center of gravity shifted toward making these building blocks fast, composable, and economically robust. Payment-channel and cross-chain protocols matured with A2L's anonymous atomic locks (S&P 2021) and Universal Atomic Swaps (S&P 2022), while MAD-HTLC (S&P 2021) reframed security in game-theoretic, incentive terms by showing HTLCs are cheap to attack. Consensus reached a new plateau with DAG-based Bullshark (CCS 2022) and throughput-oblivious Dumbo-NG (CCS 2022), and Ebb-and-Flow Protocols (S&P 2021) resolved the availability-versus-finality dilemma. Distributed randomness and key generation became headline systems results through Spurt (S&P 2022) and Practical Asynchronous DKG (S&P 2022). The same period saw cryptographic protocols meet machine learning, as Eluding Secure Aggregation (CCS 2022) showed how a malicious server can break federated-learning privacy. The arc, then, runs from sharded ledgers and deployable signing schemes, through rigorous formal analysis and high-profile real-world breaks, to today's emphasis on scalable asynchronous consensus, incentive-aware channel protocols, and threshold infrastructure that underpins the whole stack.
